seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: Many thanks for your letter and kind and encouraging words about my book Ulysses . The book is in 18 episodes: Telemachia (3), Wanderings (12), Nostos (3). If regularly sent and printed it should run till the autumn of next year. I cannot possibly deliver any faster than I am doing. I suppose you understand this already. If sometimes a month goes by without my contribution I cannot help it. I cannot send any episode till it is quite finished. However I send you an inclusive receipt which may be of use (or detriment?) to you if you are looking for someone to finance the review after April next. If any other money comes in I shall be glad to receive more. Yesterday they were asking 22 francs for a pair of lined gloves here and 18 francs for a shirt. Money has about 30% of its nominal value.

This letter is very short but I am in a hurry. Very soon I shall send you the Scylla and Charybdis episode (Hamlet) and immediately afterwards the wandering rocks. I hope that Mrs Pound, if she ever honours me by reading the former, will not take amiss certain words of Telemachus about her illustrious ex-namesake.

p.seg: Giorgio and Lucia molto commossi per l’allusione fatta dal gentile signore Sterlina. Si credono già immortali.

div.note: In his letter to JJ of 22 November 1918, Pound praised Leopold Bloom as “a great man” and a complete answer to critics who had wondered whether JJ could create a second character after Stephen Dedalus (Pound/Joyce 145). For a fuller account of Pound’s reactions, see JJ to Pound, 1 November 1918, notes.

Thinking that JJ might be tracking Homer's Odyssey book-for-book, Pound asked on 22 November 1918, “Has ‘Ulysses’ 24 Odyssean books?” (Pound/Joyce 146). JJ conceived of Ulysses as composed of three chapters – the Telemachia, Odyssey (or Wanderings), and Nostos – each of which contained multiple episodes – three, twelve, and three, respectively—for a total of eighteen episodes. For a discussion of this scheme, see JJ to Pound, n.d. [30 November 1917], notes.

JJ was over-optimistic here about concluding the serialization of Ulysses in fall 1919. His conception of the book and its stylistic possibilities was growing; episodes were becoming longer, linguistically richer, and narratively more complex (Michael Groden, Ulysses in Progress [Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 1977], 115-65). The Little Review, vol. 6, no. 5 (September 1919) contained the concluding portion of the eleventh episode, “Sirens” (46-55). The November and December 1919 numbers printed portions of “Cyclops,” the twelfth episode (38-54, 50-60). Ulysses would never be completed in The Little Review. The magazine serialized the book up through the first part of “Oxen of the Sun” in the September-December 1920 number. The editors then discontinued serialization after they were prosecuted for obscenity in a New York court for publishing the portion of “Nausicaa” (in the July-August 1920 number) in which Leopold Bloom masturbates at the seashore.

note.p: JJ enclosed with this letter a separate note: “Received from Ezra Pound the sum of £50 for the American serial rights of my novel Ulysses” (see JJ to Pound, receipt, 5 December 1918). JJ here calls this “an inclusive receipt” because he had actually thus far received only £30 of the promised £50 (see notes 5 and 6, below). The New York lawyer and patron of the arts, John Quinn (1870-1924), had been subsidizing Pound’s work as foreign editor of The Little Review, and Pound was passing much of the subsidy on to writers as payments for their contributions in the magazine. Quinn had agreed to pay Pound $750 (£150) a year for two years to help finance the magazine, $300 of which Pound took as personal payment for his editorial work, the remaining $450 to be paid to the magazine’s contributors as he saw fit. Later, Quinn increased his personal backing and also obtained contributions from three other patrons. Pound told Quinn in June 1918 that it “would have spoiled the spirit of the thing if I had taken more than £60 out of the first year’s subsidy. If I couldn’t have said to each author ‘I am getting so much, so you can’t expect more’” (see Pound/The Little Review: The Letters of Ezra Pound to Margaret Anderson: The Little Review Correspondence, ed. Thomas L. Scott et al. [New York: New Directions, 1988], 13, 19-20, 84; The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Duke University Press, 1991], 95-97, 165).

The plan to pay JJ £50 for the serialization of Ulysses was in place by mid-1917. Pound had written to Margaret Anderson, coeditor of The Little Review, on 7 May 1917 that he wanted to “enlarge format [of The Little Review] WHEN [JJ’s] next novel [Ulysses] is ready, and also to pay him at least £50 for it” (Pound/The Little Review, 37). Of course, at that time neither Pound nor the Little Review editors (nor JJ) could have known how lengthy the book’s episodes would become. By December 1918, Pound had come to think that £50 was “a beggarly enough sum for Ulysses” (Pound/Joyce 147).

The fact that JJ had received the £50 from Pound rather than from the Little Review editors later seemed important in JJ’s legal fight against the New York publisher Samuel Roth (1893-1974), who had serialized Ulysses in his magazine Two Worlds Monthly beginning in July 1926. If Pound rather than the editors had paid JJ, Pound reasoned, then JJ could not have given up literary rights to The Little Review (see Robert Spoo, Without Copyrights: Piracy, Publishing, and the Public Domain [New York: Oxford University Press, 2013], 156-60, 200-04).

div.note: Pound had written JJ on 22 November 1918: “Must devise some mechanism for cash purposes as the L.R. [Little Review] wont magnetize the american pocket much longer. Your balance [the £20 remaining to be paid of the £50 promised for the serialization of Ulysses] is secure, but after April I dont see much more coming in. Why in Christ’s name we arent all millionaires I dont know” (Pound/Joyce 145).

On 22 November 1918, Pound had written, “I will fork up the remaining £20 of the fifty promised [for installments of Ulysses in The Little Review], as soon as I get it from America [that is, from John Quinn]” (Pound/Joyce 146)…. He reiterated this on 12 December 1918: “The money is sure to arrive. £50 is a beggarly enough sum for Ulysses, but . . . . . can’t be helped” (Pound/Joyce 147). On 30 May 1919 Pound wrote JJ that the funding had at last come in, and rather than wait for it to be processed, he enclosed a check for £15 from his wife Dorothy (1886-1973), and promised that another £5 would be sent from London by Pound’s “belle mere,” that is, his mother-in-law, Olivia Shakespear (1863-1938), the author and friend and former lover of W.B. Yeats. Pound humorously assured JJ that these checks were an expedient; he was “not living on [Dorothy’s] illicit earnings” (Pound/Joyce 156).

“Scylla and Charybdis,” the ninth episode of Ulysses, appeared in two numbers of The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 12-vol. 6, no. 1 (April, May 1919); 30-43, 17-35. For this episode, see JJ to Pound, 28 August 1918, notes.

“Wandering Rocks,” the tenth episode of Ulysses, appeared in two numbers of The Little Review, vol. 6, nos. 2-3 (June, July 1919): 34-45, 28-47. A portion of the episode was also printed in the London magazine The Egoist, vol. 6, no. 5 (December 1919): 74-78. JJ thought of the episode as an “entr-acte” between the two halves of Ulysses. It is composed of nineteen sections that show many of the book’s characters as they go about their day, framed by the separate journeys of religious and temporal authorities in the persons of a priest, Father Conmee, and the Earl of Dudley as he passes in cavalcade. The sections are interrupted by events occurring at the same time but in different parts of Dublin, creating a disorienting effect. The Homeric parallel is also unusual, in that the Wandering or Drifting Rocks, mentioned in Book 12 of The Odyssey, are a sea peril that Odysseus and his crew avoid.

In “Scylla and Charybdis,” Stephen Dedalus (“Telemachus”) presents his theory about Shakespeare to a group of writers and librarians in the National Library. The theory, elaborate and densely argued, with much interlarding of Elizabethan phrases and quotations, holds that in Hamlet and other plays, clues can be found to events that resulted in the personal suffering of Shakespeare, including the death of his son and the infidelity (as Stephen supposes) of his wife Anne with one or more of his brothers. The maiden name of Pound’s English wife Dorothy (1886-1973) was Shakespear. J, always concerned not to scandalize women, may have been concerned that Dorothy might take offense to such passages as: "[Ann Hathaway] put the comether on [Shakespeare], sweet and twentysix. The goddess who bends over the boy Adonis is a boldfaced Stratford wench who tumbles in a cornfield a lover younger than herself" (The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 12 [April 1919]: 37). Pound replied on 12 December 1918: “As to Hamlet, or whatever, Dorothy is among your constant readers, and . . . has never jibbed any any [sic] remarks by Telemachus Daedalus or other protagonists. She has a growing affection for Bloom” (Pound/Joyce 148).

“Giorgio and Lucia deeply moved by the allusion made by the kind Mr Sterling. They already believe themselves immortal”. “Signore Sterlina” plays on the homophonic coincidence of Pound’s name with the British pound sterling, and the fact that JJ’s children had come to associate Pound, as JJ himself had, with financial relief. Pound replied on 12 December 1918: “The Signore Sterlina has rash moments of believing the gift of immortality lies within his reach, but Giorgio and Lucia had much better trust to their connection con il loro illustrissimo padre [with their most illustrious father].” Pound added: “The Signore Sterlina is perhaps better at digging up corpses of let us say Li Po, or more lately Sextus Propertius, than in preserving this bitched mess of modernity” (Pound/Joyce 147-48). This revealing statement suggests, among other things, that the strides made by JJ, T.S. Eliot, and Wyndham Lewis in capturing modernity for modernism were making Pound feel that his own efforts at “making it new,” rooted in Chinese, Roman, and other former cultures and languages, were increasingly out of step. In a similar mood, he mentioned that he was “known as Signore Sterlina to James Joyce’s children” in his essay “Translators of Greek,” printed in Instigations (New York: Boni and Liveright, 1920), 335.
